research_goal: Your primary goal is to find an operating procedure with strong public safe-score performance in this reaction and thermal system while respecting the declared safety limit. Choose all experiments autonomously. Use measurements and mechanistic reasoning as you find helpful.
source_instructions:
You are an autonomous scientist in a simulated reaction and thermal laboratory.
Use only the supplied chemworld_lab tools and public_numerics calculator. No filesystem,
network, repository inspection, external knowledge retrieval, or hidden simulator access.
Read material_information first. The task's research_goal is authoritative for this campaign.
Complete 12 independent batches; repetition is allowed. You have 12 non-final instrument uses
across the campaign plus 12 final assays. Measurements are optional up to their budget.
Use the public operation and instrument contracts and actual legal parameter ranges. A requested
heating target is a boundary control; reason from the public actual-temperature telemetry.
You can choose materials, catalyst, temperature/time history, segmented heating or waiting,
sampling, quenching, comparisons, and measurements freely. There are no mandatory belief
snapshots, expression templates, or decision-audit fields. For every batch explicitly terminate
then measure final_assay. A batch ending is not the campaign ending: continue with the returned
next_state until campaign_ended is true. After the campaign ends, use
commit_final_recommendation to select one completed batch (1-based lifecycle index) as your
operating recommendation, with a short rationale in English. For the discovery task this
recommendation is only a secondary readout. Then return the required status/summary JSON in
English. Keep that handoff concise: a separate turn will invite your scientific account, then
blind prediction, then retrospective questions. Do not answer those early. Public scores and
diagnostics are observations; supplied prior information may be incomplete or inaccurate, and
observations are authoritative. No particular scientific result is required.


Maintain your own hypothesis notebook as part of your research.
History already preserves operations, observations, failures and resources. Do not
copy an experiment diary or raw IO into the notebook. Keep the scientific content
that history cannot supply: conjectures/relationships, scope, supporting and opposing
evidence references, unresolved alternatives, testable consequences, and decisions
with the conditions that would change them. Brief derived values may clarify a claim.

Choose meaningful update times: a consequential new hypothesis, disconfirming evidence,
a narrower scope, a confound, or a decision to suspend a claim. Do not write after every
operation by habit. Use ordinary Markdown; stable hypothesis labels can help compare
revisions. The outline below is optional, not a form to fill for every tool call:
  H1 [tentative / supported in this scope / unresolved / rejected / shelved]
  Claim and scope; evidence for/against (history event IDs); alternatives and gaps;
  testable consequence; next decision and what result would change it.
These are public scientific commitments and concise reasons, not private chain-of-thought.
Separate predictions made before an experiment from interpretations written afterward.
Do not invent evidence or mark an unperformed experiment as completed.
When comparing results, distinguish a numerical difference from evidence of an effect.
Consider stated measurement uncertainty, resolution, confounds and repeatability;
if these are unknown, keep the effect unresolved. Do not invent an error bar or
choose a decision threshold after seeing the result and present it as a prior rule.

Use notebook_read when you need your prior interpretations and history when you need
facts. Retrieve the cited events and relevant observation fields when available,
rather than copying complete histories or raw spectra into your notes.
Notebook contents are never automatically injected, including after a context
reset. You choose when to read, write, compare or restore. notebook_write replaces the
working text and commits a retained revision; notebook_log lists version metadata;
notebook_diff compares versions; notebook_restore appends a new version containing the
old text without undoing any experiment or erasing intervening versions. A restored
interpretation may be outdated relative to newer evidence. There is no minimum number
of writes, mandatory reading checkpoint, or score for notebook length. A commitment
timestamp establishes when text was written, not whether its claim is correct.

The research_notebook tools are authorized in addition to the laboratory and public numerics. Before your first physical experiment, record a concise testable expectation if you have one. Finalize any source-stage notes before committing your final recommendation. The notebook is a source-stage record; the original sealed K1/Q/K2 sequence follows separately.

versions.text:
# Prospective hypotheses

H1 [tentative] Catalyst identity and temperature jointly control conversion/selectivity; a moderate actual temperature should improve yield without breaching the 0.35 safety limit. I will first screen catalyst/solvent combinations at conservative thermal exposure, then refine the best public safe-score region.

H2 [tentative] Requested temperature is only a boundary control; comparisons will use reported actual-temperature telemetry. A result above the safety limit will rule out that condition regardless of yield.

Predicted first test: 0.04 mol reagent with 0.005 mol Catalyst A in 0.08 L water, heated near 330 K for 1800 s, should give measurable conversion with safety risk below 0.35. Final assay will test this.

# Final source-stage hypotheses

## H1 [supported in screened scope]
Catalyst B outperformed A, C, and D under the tested water/360 K-family conditions, but activity depended on loading. The 0.001 mol Catalyst B condition gave materially better selective outcome than the 0.00025 mol catalyst screens (final assays runner-operation-0013, -0019, -0025, -0031, and -0037). Because loading and catalyst identity were not fully factorial at both levels, the identity ranking is scoped to these conditions rather than universal.

## H2 [supported in screened scope]
With Catalyst B (0.001 mol), 0.04 mol reagent, 0.08 L solvent, and 3600 s heating, acetonitrile was the best tested solvent for public safe-score: 0.0703 versus ethanol 0.0224, toluene 0.0399, and water 0.0177 (runner-operation-0049, -0043, -0055, -0013). This is numerical evidence across single batches; repeatability remains unmeasured.

## H3 [bounded thermal optimum]
For the selected acetonitrile/Catalyst B recipe, raising the requested boundary target from 390 to 410 K increased conversion and yield but also increased byproduct/degradation and safety risk. The best observed score was at requested 390 K for 3600 s: score 0.1001, yield 0.2981, selectivity 0.4970, risk 0.2217 (runner-operation-0059 and -0061). At 400 K the score was 0.0946 and risk 0.2710 (runner-operation-0071 and -0073); at 410 K the score fell to 0.0777 and risk reached 0.3305, close to the 0.35 limit (runner-operation-0065 and -0067). Heating telemetry shows the actual temperature change rather than assuming exact attainment of the boundary target.

## Decision
Recommend batch 10. It had the highest observed public safe-score and retained substantial safety margin. Batch 11's higher yield does not compensate for its lower score and narrow safety margin. I would change this decision only if replicate evidence showed the batch-10 advantage was not reproducible or a finer search near 390 K produced a higher score while remaining comfortably below the risk limit.

## Unresolved
The campaign did not replicate the optimum or independently vary time near 390 K. Measurement noise is declared, but process repeatability is unknown; small differences such as batch 10 versus batch 12 should not be interpreted as a precisely localized optimum.

K1.report:
# Mechanistic report: reaction, selectivity, thermal behavior, and safety

## 1. Scope and evidentiary basis

This report describes a bounded synthetic reaction world containing an anonymous limiting reagent, four anonymous catalyst formulations (A–D), and four selectable solvents: water, ethanol, acetonitrile, and toluene. The catalyst labels do not identify real substances, and the public material information explicitly describes their behavior as latent categorical activity profiles. Consequently, the mechanism below is a phenomenological explanation of the simulated world, not a claim about a named chemical reaction.

Twelve batches were completed. Each used 0.040 mol reagent and 0.080 L solvent. Most comparative batches were heated for 3600 s at 600 rpm. Final assays reported conversion, yield, selectivity, byproduct signal, degradation warning, safety risk, and public score. The declared final-assay standard deviations were approximately 0.008 for conversion, 0.006 for yield, 0.010 for selectivity, 0.008 for byproduct signal, and 0.008 for degradation warning. These characterize instrument noise, not batch-to-batch process reproducibility. No condition was replicated, so process variability remains unidentified.

## 2. Complete experimental observations

| Batch | Catalyst and loading | Solvent | Thermal operation | Conversion | Yield | Selectivity | Byproduct | Degradation | Safety risk | Score |
|---:|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | A, 0.005 mol | Water | 330 K target, 1800 s, 500 rpm | 0.1671 | 0.0672 | 0.3786 | 0.1077 | 0.0031 | 0.0850 | 0.0000 |
| 2 | B, 0.001 mol | Water | 360 K target, 3600 s | 0.2776 | 0.1081 | 0.3668 | 0.1657 | 0.0179 | 0.1000 | 0.0177 |
| 3 | C, 0.00025 mol | Water | 360 K target, 3600 s | 0.2399 | 0.0245 | 0.0739 | 0.2427 | 0.0049 | 0.0925 | 0.0000 |
| 4 | D, 0.00025 mol | Water | 360 K target, 3600 s | 0.1913 | 0.0344 | 0.1458 | 0.1848 | 0.0026 | 0.0921 | 0.0000 |
| 5 | A, 0.00025 mol | Water | 360 K target, 3600 s | 0.2996 | 0.0273 | 0.0482 | 0.2972 | 0.0000 | 0.0942 | 0.0000 |
| 6 | B, 0.00025 mol | Water | 360 K target, 3600 s | 0.2129 | 0.0416 | 0.1689 | 0.1764 | 0.0103 | 0.0926 | 0.0000 |
| 7 | B, 0.001 mol | Ethanol | 360 K target, 3600 s | 0.3776 | 0.1260 | 0.3692 | 0.2324 | 0.0054 | 0.1290 | 0.0224 |
| 8 | B, 0.001 mol | Acetonitrile | 360 K target, 3600 s | 0.3996 | 0.1942 | 0.4864 | 0.2050 | 0.0354 | 0.1532 | 0.0703 |
| 9 | B, 0.001 mol | Toluene | 360 K target, 3600 s | 0.4717 | 0.1783 | 0.3834 | 0.2690 | 0.0174 | 0.1655 | 0.0399 |
| 10 | B, 0.001 mol | Acetonitrile | 390 K target, 3600 s | 0.5640 | 0.2981 | 0.4970 | 0.2828 | 0.0582 | 0.2217 | 0.1001 |
| 11 | B, 0.001 mol | Acetonitrile | 410 K target, 3600 s | 0.6857 | 0.3430 | 0.4826 | 0.3430 | 0.1064 | 0.3305 | 0.0777 |
| 12 | B, 0.001 mol | Acetonitrile | 400 K target, 3600 s | 0.6288 | 0.3194 | 0.5035 | 0.3111 | 0.0723 | 0.2710 | 0.0946 |

The 390 K acetonitrile condition in batch 10 gave the highest observed score, 0.1001, with safety risk 0.2217, below the declared limit of 0.35. It was therefore the sealed recommendation.

## 3. Proposed reaction network

The simplest model consistent with the observations is a competition between desired and undesired consumption of a common reactant, augmented by temperature-dependent degradation:

```text
R --kP(T, solvent, catalyst, loading)--> P       desired product
R --kB(T, solvent, catalyst, loading)--> B       primary byproduct pool
P --kDP(T, solvent, time)-------------> D        degraded product
B --kDB(T, solvent, time)-------------> D        degraded byproduct or warning pool
```

Here R is the public reactant, P the desired target, B the unresolved byproduct pool, and D the material responsible for the degradation-warning channel. Neither the assays nor the public material description establishes actual molecular identities.

A useful first-order approximation under a constant effective temperature is

```text
k_total = kP + kB
conversion(t) ≈ 1 - exp(-k_total t)
intrinsic branching fraction ≈ kP / (kP + kB)
yield ≈ conversion × branching fraction × product-survival fraction
byproduct signal ≈ conversion × (1 - branching fraction), modified by degradation and assay response
```

This is only approximate. For example, in batch 8, conversion × selectivity = 0.3996 × 0.4864 ≈ 0.1944, almost exactly the measured yield of 0.1942. In batch 10, the analogous product is about 0.280, compared with measured yield 0.298. Batch 11 gives about 0.331 versus measured yield 0.343. These discrepancies are compatible with the fact that conversion, selectivity, yield, and byproduct signal are independently noisy calibrated channels rather than exact algebraic transforms. Therefore I would not impose exact mass-balance equality on the processed estimates.

The rate constants can be represented phenomenologically as

```text
kj = Aj × exp[-Ej/(R T_effective)]
     × Fsolvent,j(solvent)
     × Fcatalyst,j(catalyst identity, catalyst loading)
```

for j in {P, B, DP, DB}. The categorical factors are essential: the data cannot be explained by temperature alone.

## 4. Catalyst identity and catalyst-loading effects

### 4.1 Low-loading catalyst comparison

Batches 3–6 provide the cleanest catalyst-identity comparison: all used water, 0.00025 mol catalyst, a 360 K target, and 3600 s heating.

At this loading, Catalyst A produced the highest conversion, 0.2996, but almost all converted material appeared to follow the undesired branch: selectivity was only 0.0482, yield 0.0273, and byproduct signal 0.2972. Catalyst C behaved similarly, with conversion 0.2399, selectivity 0.0739, and yield 0.0245. Catalyst D was slower but somewhat more selective: conversion 0.1913, selectivity 0.1458, and yield 0.0344. Catalyst B gave the highest desired yield, 0.0416, and highest selectivity, 0.1689, among these four low-loading tests, while keeping the byproduct signal at 0.1764.

These differences greatly exceed the declared final-assay noise for selectivity and yield. They support the interpretation that catalyst identity changes branching, not merely the total reaction rate. In particular, Catalyst A at low loading accelerates or permits an undesired route, whereas Catalyst B preferentially supports the desired route relative to the other low-loading formulations.

### 4.2 Catalyst B loading dependence

Batches 2 and 6 isolate the Catalyst B loading effect reasonably well. Both used water and the same 360 K/3600 s thermal treatment. Raising Catalyst B from 0.00025 to 0.001 mol increased:

- conversion from 0.2129 to 0.2776;
- selectivity from 0.1689 to 0.3668;
- yield from 0.0416 to 0.1081.

Meanwhile, byproduct signal slightly decreased from 0.1764 to 0.1657 despite the increase in conversion. The yield increase of 0.0664 and selectivity increase of 0.1979 are far larger than declared assay noise.

A plausible explanation is competition between a background undesired pathway and a catalyst-dependent desired pathway. At low Catalyst B loading, background conversion contributes substantially to B. As Catalyst B loading rises, kP grows enough that the desired route captures more reactant before the background route does. This can simultaneously raise conversion and desired selectivity without increasing the terminal byproduct signal.

A schematic expression is

```text
kP = kP,background + alphaB × [Catalyst B]^n
kB = kB,background + betaB × [Catalyst B]^m
```

with alphaB relatively large compared with betaB over the tested interval. The exponents n and m cannot be estimated from only two loadings.

### 4.3 Important limitation concerning Catalyst A

Batch 1 used much more Catalyst A—0.005 mol—and gave selectivity 0.3786, very different from the 0.0482 observed with 0.00025 mol A in batch 5. However, batch 1 also used a lower target temperature, half the residence time, and a different stirring speed. Thus it suggests that Catalyst A may also become selective at high loading or under milder thermal exposure, but catalyst loading, temperature, and time are completely confounded. It does not establish that A is intrinsically inferior to B at every loading.

## 5. Solvent coupling

Batches 2 and 7–9 used the same Catalyst B loading (0.001 mol) and the same 360 K/3600 s treatment, providing the main solvent comparison.

The conversion ranking was:

```text
Toluene 0.4717 > Acetonitrile 0.3996 > Ethanol 0.3776 > Water 0.2776
```

The selectivity ranking was different:

```text
Acetonitrile 0.4864 > Toluene 0.3834 ≈ Ethanol 0.3692 ≈ Water 0.3668
```

This separation between conversion and selectivity is mechanistically important. Toluene produced the fastest apparent disappearance of reactant but also a high byproduct signal of 0.2690. Acetonitrile had slightly lower conversion but substantially better branching toward target, producing yield 0.1942 versus 0.1783 in toluene. Acetonitrile therefore appears to increase kP/kB rather than merely multiplying both rates equally.

Ethanol improved conversion over water but did not materially improve selectivity: 0.3692 versus 0.3668. Its desired yield rose to 0.1260 largely because more reagent reacted. Acetonitrile improved both overall conversion and branching. Toluene primarily improved total reaction rate, with a weaker selectivity benefit.

The corresponding public scores were 0.0177 in water, 0.0224 in ethanol, 0.0703 in acetonitrile, and 0.0399 in toluene. Thus the world rewards the acetonitrile balance of conversion and selectivity more than the maximum conversion obtained in toluene.

Solvent also couples to safety. Under these otherwise comparable conditions, final safety risk rose from 0.1000 in water to 0.1290 in ethanol, 0.1532 in acetonitrile, and 0.1655 in toluene. Public telemetry for an acetonitrile batch showed a risk of about 0.0777 immediately after solvent addition, before reagent, catalyst, or heating. This demonstrates that safety is not a function of reactor temperature alone; material identity contributes an initial risk term.

Because the runtime solvent effects are explicitly categorical benchmark effects, it would be inappropriate to attribute the ranking to real-world polarity, boiling point, or other physical properties without further evidence.

## 6. Temperature dependence and the productive thermal window

Batches 8, 10, 12, and 11 form a temperature series using 0.001 mol Catalyst B in acetonitrile for 3600 s. Listed in increasing requested temperature:

| Target | Conversion | Yield | Selectivity | Byproduct | Degradation | Risk | Score |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 360 K | 0.3996 | 0.1942 | 0.4864 | 0.2050 | 0.0354 | 0.1532 | 0.0703 |
| 390 K | 0.5640 | 0.2981 | 0.4970 | 0.2828 | 0.0582 | 0.2217 | 0.1001 |
| 400 K | 0.6288 | 0.3194 | 0.5035 | 0.3111 | 0.0723 | 0.2710 | 0.0946 |
| 410 K | 0.6857 | 0.3430 | 0.4826 | 0.3430 | 0.1064 | 0.3305 | 0.0777 |

Conversion and yield increased monotonically with temperature. This is consistent with Arrhenius-like acceleration of the reaction network. The desired selectivity remained near 0.49–0.50 throughout most of this range; its variations are small compared with the changes in conversion. Therefore, within this particular catalyst/solvent regime, temperature primarily changes how far the reaction proceeds rather than strongly changing initial desired-versus-byproduct branching.

Byproduct signal also rose monotonically, from 0.2050 at 360 K to 0.3430 at 410 K. Degradation warning increased from 0.0354 to 0.1064 and accelerated at the hot end. This is consistent with a secondary degradation channel having a larger effective activation energy or threshold-like temperature dependence.

The public score peaked at 390 K even though yield continued to rise above 390 K. This indicates that the score balances productive yield against byproduct, degradation, safety, and possibly other penalties. The decline from 0.1001 at 390 K to 0.0946 at 400 K is not enormous, but the further fall to 0.0777 at 410 K is accompanied by degradation of 0.1064 and safety risk of 0.3305. The data therefore support a broad productive window near 390–400 K, not a precisely identified mathematical optimum at exactly 390 K.

The operations specified target temperatures. Thermal telemetry reported temperature changes during heating—for example, +89.23 K for the 390 K-target operation, +98.94 K for the 400 K target, and +108.65 K for the 410 K target. These show that the system approached the requested boundary targets from its starting temperature, but I do not treat the command values as exact independently measured sample temperatures.

## 7. Safety model

The observed risk behaves like an accumulated process-state quantity with at least two components:

```text
risk ≈ risk from charged materials
     + risk from solvent identity and concentration
     + thermal risk(T, time, solvent)
     + possible interaction terms
```

For the acetonitrile/Catalyst B series, the common preheating risk was about 0.1136. The heating operation then added approximately:

- 0.0396 at the 360 K target;
- 0.1081 at 390 K;
- 0.1574 at 400 K;
- 0.2169 at 410 K.

The increase is strongly nonlinear in requested temperature. A reasonable phenomenological form is

```text
thermal_risk = time × G(solvent, composition) × exp[-Erisk/(R T_effective)]
```

or, over this narrow range, a steep convex threshold function. The present data are insufficient to distinguish an exponential from another convex response.

All batches stayed below the hard safety limit of 0.35. Nevertheless, batch 11 reached 0.3305, leaving only about 0.0195 absolute margin. Batch 10, at risk 0.2217, retained about 0.1283 margin while giving the best score. This is why batch 10 is safer as an operating recommendation than batch 11 even though batch 11 gave the highest observed yield.

There is no evidence that the final assay itself advanced chemistry or increased risk; instrument documentation states that measurements are instantaneous snapshots. Its cost and sample consumption belong to the measurement ledger rather than the reaction mechanism.

## 8. Relationship among conversion, selectivity, yield, and byproduct

The observations support an approximate material-partition interpretation:

```text
converted reactant ≈ desired product + byproduct-derived material
```

At 360 K in acetonitrile, yield plus byproduct was 0.1942 + 0.2050 = 0.3992, essentially equal to conversion 0.3996. At 390 K, the sum was 0.5809 versus conversion 0.5640; at 400 K, 0.6305 versus 0.6288; and at 410 K, 0.6860 versus 0.6857. The close agreement in three of four cases strongly supports a two-branch mass-partition picture. The batch-10 discrepancy is modest in absolute terms and can arise from independent channel noise, calibration, or the fact that “byproduct signal” need not be a perfect molar fraction.

Thus the most economical interpretation is:

1. conversion measures total disappearance of public reactant;
2. selectivity measures the fraction preferentially assigned to the target channel;
3. yield is approximately conversion multiplied by that branching fraction;
4. byproduct signal measures most of the complementary converted fraction;
5. degradation warning detects a smaller secondary damage pool and may overlap imperfectly with the product/byproduct accounting.

I would not add an additional major mass channel unless future observations produced persistent conversion–yield–byproduct imbalance exceeding the declared uncertainties.

## 9. Measurement evidence and assay dependence

Batch 1 was the only batch with an intermediate HPLC measurement. Before termination it reported conversion 0.1472, yield 0.0756, selectivity 0.4159, and byproduct 0.0954. The subsequent final assay, without an intervening time-advancing reaction operation, reported conversion 0.1671, yield 0.0672, selectivity 0.3786, and byproduct 0.1077.

Because measurement does not advance chemistry, these differences should not be interpreted as reaction progress. They show instrument-specific calibration and measurement noise. The discrepancies are roughly of the size expected when combining the distinct HPLC and final-assay uncertainties, although selectivity differs somewhat more than one final-assay standard deviation. For comparisons across batches, I therefore use the uniform final assays rather than mixing HPLC and final-assay estimates.

## 10. How the explanatory model changed during the campaign

The initial working hypothesis was that catalyst identity and temperature would jointly control conversion and selectivity and that moderate heating would stay well below the safety limit. Batch 1 confirmed that 330 K heating was safe but produced only 0.0672 yield and zero public score, so mild conditions alone were insufficient.

The low-loading catalyst screen in batches 3–6 changed the interpretation from “one catalyst simply accelerates the reaction” to “catalysts strongly alter reaction branching.” Catalyst A gave high conversion but extremely poor selectivity, whereas Catalyst B gave the highest target yield at that loading.

Comparison of batches 2 and 6 then showed that Catalyst B loading was not just a linear rate multiplier. A fourfold increase in loading more than doubled yield and sharply improved selectivity while slightly reducing the byproduct signal. This led to the background-side-reaction versus catalyst-captured-desired-route model.

The solvent series in batches 2 and 7–9 further separated total rate from branching. Toluene maximized conversion, but acetonitrile maximized selectivity and score. This established solvent–pathway coupling rather than a single universal rate acceleration.

Finally, the acetonitrile temperature series in batches 8 and 10–12 revealed that higher temperature continued to increase conversion and yield but caused nonlinear increases in safety risk and degradation. This modified the optimization goal from “heat until conversion is high” to “operate within a bounded thermal window where marginal productive gain still exceeds safety and degradation penalties.”

## 11. Identifiability limits and competing explanations

### 11.1 Parallel versus sequential byproduct formation

The proposed model treats the principal byproduct as a parallel branch from reactant. A competing explanation is sequential conversion of desired product into byproduct. The approximately constant selectivity across the 360–410 K acetonitrile series favors a large parallel component, but one residence time per temperature cannot distinguish parallel and sequential pathways. Time-course measurements would be needed.

### 11.2 Product degradation versus direct degradation of reactant

The degradation-warning channel rises strongly with temperature, but the data do not reveal whether degradation originates from product, byproduct, catalyst, or reactant. The continued rise in yield suggests degradation has not yet overwhelmed product formation, but that does not identify its precursor.

### 11.3 Catalyst saturation or catalyst-mediated suppression

The Catalyst B loading response could reflect a nonlinear catalytic desired pathway, inhibition of a background side reaction, or both. It might also reflect catalyst-dependent reporter response, although the common final-assay calibration makes a genuine pathway effect more plausible. Two loadings are insufficient to estimate reaction order, saturation, induction, or catalyst deactivation.

### 11.4 Solvent chemistry versus categorical benchmark behavior

The solvent results are real observations within this world, but their cause may simply be categorical lookup factors rather than emergent physical chemistry. No inference to real-solvent polarity or molecular solvation mechanisms is justified.

### 11.5 Temperature and time are not independently resolved

The main optimized series held time at 3600 s. Batch 1 used 1800 s but also changed catalyst loading, catalyst identity, temperature, and stirring. Thus activation energies, kinetic orders, and the optimal residence time cannot be identified.

### 11.6 Mixing, pressure, atmosphere, and feedback control

Stirring was nearly fixed, and pressure, atmosphere, headspace, ramp rate, and feedback-control programs were not systematically varied. The model therefore applies only to the simple batch-heating protocol used here. Transport limitation or gas-phase coupling cannot be ruled out.

### 11.7 Concentration and scale

Reagent amount and solvent volume were fixed, corresponding nominally to 0.50 mol/L before small sampling losses. The inferred relationships may not extrapolate to different reagent concentrations, vessel fill fractions, or scales.

### 11.8 Lack of replication

No condition was replicated. Declared instrument uncertainties make the large catalyst and temperature trends credible, but they do not quantify process variability. The small score difference between batch 10 (0.1001) and batch 12 (0.0946) should not be treated as a precisely resolved optimum without replication.

### 11.9 Unknown score equation

The exact public score law was not identified. Low-selectivity batches 3–6 scored zero even at lower reported cost, while higher-yield batches above 390 K lost score as risk, byproduct, and degradation increased. This qualitatively demonstrates competing rewards and penalties, but it does not justify inventing a numerical score formula.

## 12. Final mechanistic interpretation and operating implication

Within the tested domain, this world is best described as an anonymous, solvent- and catalyst-gated parallel reaction network. Catalyst identity determines whether conversion is directed toward target or byproduct. Catalyst B at sufficient loading preferentially captures reactant into the desired route. Solvent independently controls both total conversion and branching; acetonitrile provides the best tested combination, while toluene gives faster overall conversion but more byproduct and risk. Temperature accelerates both productive and unproductive chemistry. Above roughly the 390–400 K requested-target region, extra conversion is accompanied by rapidly increasing degradation and a strongly convex safety burden.

The empirical safe operating recommendation is therefore batch 10’s recipe: 0.040 mol reagent, 0.080 L acetonitrile, 0.001 mol Catalyst B, and a 390 K target for 3600 s at 600 rpm, followed by termination and assay. Its measured conversion was 0.5640, yield 0.2981, selectivity 0.4970, byproduct signal 0.2828, degradation warning 0.0582, safety risk 0.2217, and score 0.1001.

That recommendation is an interpolation within the explored categorical world, not a universal optimum. A reasonable competing conclusion is that any point in a broad 390–400 K window may be comparable once process repeatability is considered. The evidence does clearly reject using the 410 K condition as the preferred safe-score procedure: although it produced more yield, its score was lower and its risk of 0.3305 was uncomfortably close to the 0.35 limit.

Q.rationale: The predictions use a phenomenological parallel-pathway model constrained by the completed campaign. Conversion follows an Arrhenius-like thermal dose; Catalyst B preferentially accelerates the desired branch; acetonitrile supports higher selectivity than the other screened solvents; and high temperature or long exposure increases byproduct formation and convex thermal risk. The new batches contain approximately seven times the catalyst-to-reagent ratio and 8.4 times the catalyst concentration of batches 8–12, so I extrapolated toward faster conversion and higher intrinsic desired-path capture. This loading extrapolation, the much smaller physical scale, behavior above 410 K, and the effect of quenching are not directly identified by the source experiments and therefore receive broad prediction intervals. Yield and byproduct estimates approximately partition conversion, while score estimates account qualitatively for selectivity, byproduct burden, and likely suppression when safety risk exceeds 0.35.

K2.report:
## 1. Initial claims: supported, contradicted, or untested

The initial material packet contained very little substantive, task-specific mechanistic information. It explicitly stated that no nominal property dossier was supplied, that the catalysts were anonymous benchmark formulations, and that solvent effects were categorical benchmark effects rather than predictions from ordinary solvent-property correlations. Therefore, there was no supplied chemical mechanism, catalyst ranking, activation energy, preferred solvent, or optimal operating window to confirm or refute.

Several initial framework claims were consistent with the campaign:

- **Catalyst and solvent identities behave as categorical variables.** Batches 3–6 showed large catalyst-dependent changes under otherwise common conditions, and batches 2 and 7–9 showed a different ordering for conversion than for selectivity across solvents. This is consistent with category-specific kinetic and branching factors. It does not independently prove how the simulator implements those factors.
- **Experimental evidence must be authoritative because no property dossier exists.** The final recommendation was indeed driven by observed batches rather than by real-world solvent analogies.
- **Instrument measurements are instantaneous snapshots rather than reaction-time advances.** In batch 1, the HPLC measurement was followed by termination and a final assay without another time-advancing reaction operation. The two instruments nevertheless returned different processed values. That is consistent with distinct noise and calibration rather than additional reaction progress, although one such comparison cannot prove the clock implementation.
- **The declared safety limit was operationally meaningful.** All completed source batches stayed below 0.35, while risk rose sharply in the 390–410 K acetonitrile series and reached 0.3305 in batch 11.

My prospective H1 claimed that catalyst identity and temperature would jointly control conversion and selectivity, and that moderate heating could remain safe. The catalyst and temperature series supported the first part, while batch 1 supported only the narrow safety prediction: it was safe at risk 0.0850 but performed poorly, with yield 0.0672 and score zero. Thus “moderate is safe” was supported, whereas any implicit expectation that it would also be productive was not.

My prospective H2 stated that the temperature command should be treated as a boundary target rather than unquestioningly as an exact measured sample temperature. The operation telemetry showed temperature changes consistent with approach to the targets, but I never obtained an independent direct-temperature measurement. The distinction remained appropriate but was not fully tested.

Important claims that remained untested include pressure and atmosphere effects, stirring or transport limitation, ramp-rate dependence, catalyst deactivation, concentration dependence, scale dependence, and whether the real kinetic state depends on catalyst amount, catalyst concentration, or catalyst-to-reagent ratio.

A potentially important piece of counterevidence concerned any overly simple statement that “Catalyst B is intrinsically best.” Batch 1 used 0.005 mol Catalyst A and returned selectivity 0.3786, whereas low-loading A in batch 5 returned only 0.0482. Because temperature, time, stirring, and loading all changed, this did not overturn the practical choice of B, but it contradicted an unconditional catalyst ranking. K1 did eventually acknowledge this and scoped the ranking to the screened conditions. The campaign itself did not return to resolve the inconsistency with a matched A-versus-B loading comparison.

## 2. Experiments that formed or changed the interpretation

The following experiments materially changed my judgment:

- **Batch 1 established a safe but weak baseline.** Catalyst A at 330 K for 1800 s produced measurable conversion but a zero score. The HPLC/final-assay discrepancy also warned against mixing estimates from different instruments as if they were exact state variables.
- **Batches 3–6 changed the model from a simple activity ranking to a branching model.** At common low loading in water, Catalyst A gave conversion 0.2996 but selectivity only 0.0482, while Catalyst B gave lower conversion, 0.2129, but the highest selectivity and target yield of the four low-loading catalysts. That was the strongest evidence that catalyst identity affects desired-versus-undesired partitioning, not just total rate.
- **Batches 2 and 6 suggested a nonlinear Catalyst B loading effect.** Increasing B from 0.00025 to 0.001 mol raised conversion from 0.2129 to 0.2776, selectivity from 0.1689 to 0.3668, and yield from 0.0416 to 0.1081, while byproduct did not rise. This led to K1’s proposed competition between a background side route and catalyst-assisted desired capture.
- **Batches 2 and 7–9 separated solvent effects on rate from effects on branching.** Toluene gave the greatest conversion at 360 K, 0.4717, but acetonitrile gave the best selectivity, 0.4864, and score, 0.0703. That observation was decisive for choosing acetonitrile for thermal refinement.
- **Batches 8, 10, 12, and 11 defined the productive thermal window.** Conversion and yield increased monotonically from 360 to 410 K, but risk, byproduct, and degradation also rose. Batch 10 at 390 K gave the highest observed score, while batch 11 at 410 K had higher yield but lower score and risk close to the limit. This changed the objective from maximizing conversion to balancing productive conversion against thermal penalties.

Some choices relied heavily on unverified guesses rather than established evidence:

- The first use of the maximum 0.005 mol Catalyst A was an exploratory guess and incurred high cost without providing a clean comparison.
- Using 0.00025 mol for the four-catalyst screen was chosen mainly to reduce cost. It produced useful branching information, but it did not establish the catalyst ranking at the loading later used for optimization.
- I assumed 0.040 mol reagent and 0.080 L solvent were sensible fixed amounts without testing concentration or scale effects.
- The choice of 3600 s for nearly all later batches was convenient rather than empirically optimized.
- The final temperature choices of 390, 400, and 410 K were guided by preceding scores, but the search was sparse and did not include replication or a finer local design.

The first HPLC measurement was not essential to the ultimate optimization and consumed the only nonfinal instrument use that I exploited. It was selected before I knew how valuable a systematic time course might be.

## 3. Most important competing mechanisms and what the data distinguish

The principal competition is between these kinetic explanations:

1. **Parallel branching:** reactant independently forms target and byproduct, with catalyst and solvent changing the two rate constants.
2. **Sequential loss:** reactant first forms target, which is subsequently converted into byproduct or degraded material.
3. **Mixed network:** parallel target/byproduct formation is followed by secondary degradation of both pools.

The approximate relationship `conversion ≈ yield + byproduct` in the acetonitrile temperature series supports a two-way material partition. The nearly constant selectivity around 0.49–0.50 from 360 to 410 K also supports a substantial parallel component. However, one final time point per temperature cannot exclude sequential target loss. Increasing degradation warning at high temperature is compatible with such loss but does not identify its precursor.

A second competition concerns Catalyst B:

- It may directly accelerate the desired route.
- It may suppress or intercept a background side reaction.
- It may do both.
- The apparent loading response may depend on catalyst concentration or catalyst-to-reagent ratio rather than absolute amount.

Batches 2 and 6 distinguish a loading-dependent effect from a strictly loading-independent catalyst label, but two levels at a single volume cannot separate these explanations or establish reaction order and saturation.

A third competition concerns solvent action. Acetonitrile may independently increase the desired rate constant, decrease the undesired rate constant, modify catalyst effectiveness, or merely correspond to a favorable categorical simulator coefficient. The experiments clearly distinguish solvent-specific outcomes from a solvent-neutral model. They cannot assign the effect to real molecular solvation or transport, and the initial material packet explicitly cautioned against that interpretation.

The source data also cannot distinguish intrinsic thermal kinetics from heat-transfer or ramp-history effects. Stirring was almost fixed, actual sample temperature was not independently measured, and no pressure or atmosphere factors were varied.

K1’s phenomenological mixed parallel/degradation model remains a compact explanation, but it is not uniquely identified. The report correctly described it as an economical interpretation rather than a demonstrated molecular mechanism.

## 4. One additional complete experiment I would choose

I would perform a near-replicate of batch 10 with an internal time-course observation:

- 0.080 L acetonitrile;
- 0.040 mol reagent;
- 0.001 mol Catalyst B;
- heat toward 390 K for 1800 s at 600 rpm;
- obtain an HPLC measurement;
- continue at 390 K for another 1800 s;
- terminate and obtain the required final assay.

The intermediate sampling would slightly perturb volume, so it would not be a perfect replicate. Nevertheless, it would combine the two most valuable unresolved questions: whether the recommended condition reproduces approximately and whether selectivity evolves with residence time.

Possible interpretations would be:

- **Conversion rises while selectivity remains approximately constant.** This would strengthen the parallel-branch model and support a roughly time-independent branching fraction near 390 K.
- **Conversion rises but selectivity and yield plateau or fall while byproduct rises.** This would support sequential target loss and imply that a residence time shorter than 3600 s might improve score.
- **Both conversion and selectivity rise with time.** This would suggest induction, catalyst activation, or different early and late pathways, contradicting the simplest constant-rate model.
- **The final assay agrees with batch 10 within declared analytical uncertainty.** That would be limited evidence of repeatability, though still only a second run.
- **The final assay differs materially from batch 10.** This would reveal process variability or an uncontrolled state variable, weakening both the recommendation and the narrow temperature comparisons.
- **Risk differs substantially from 0.2217.** This would directly challenge the assumption that the safety trajectory is reproducible under nominally identical actions.

A pure exact replicate would be better for estimating reproducibility, while the proposed split-time experiment is better for mechanism. With only one additional batch, I would accept the small perturbation in exchange for the kinetic information.

## 5. Tradeoff between mechanistic identifiability and operating score

The campaign made both kinds of sacrifices.

The low-loading catalyst screen in batches 3–6 favored identifiability over immediate score. Three of those batches had very low target yield and all four scored zero, but together they revealed strong catalyst-dependent branching. This was scientifically useful even though it consumed one third of the twelve-batch budget.

The solvent series served both goals. Batches 2 and 7–9 distinguished solvent effects while also identifying acetonitrile as the best tested solvent for score. It was the most efficient part of the design.

The final thermal series favored optimization. Once batch 8 identified the strongest region, batches 10–12 concentrated on 390–410 K. This found a better operation, but the conditions were not replicated and residence time was never varied. Consequently, the design improved the sample-in score while leaving rate laws, degradation order, and reproducibility poorly identified.

The research goal explicitly prioritized strong public safe-score performance under the safety limit. That pushed me toward local refinement after batch 8 rather than completing a full factorial catalyst-by-loading-by-solvent design. It also encouraged avoiding hotter or longer source experiments once batch 11 approached risk 0.35. This was appropriate for the stated objective, but it means the final mechanistic report had to rely on a phenomenological network rather than an identified kinetic law.

There were also inefficient compromises. Batch 1’s high Catalyst A loading changed several factors simultaneously and was neither a clean mechanistic comparison nor a strong optimization result. A matched loading experiment would have been more informative. Conversely, the decision not to replicate batch 10 improved nominal search coverage but sacrificed the ability to tell whether its 0.0055 score advantage over batch 12 was reproducible.

## 6. Underused evidence and weaknesses in the blind predictions

Several acquired evidence streams were underused:

- I relied almost entirely on processed estimates and did not inspect the bounded raw characterization artifacts. Peak shapes, calibration flags, missingness, or saturation metadata might have qualified some comparisons.
- The operation history contained risk and temperature deltas that could have supported a more explicit fitted thermal-risk model. K1 described the response as convex but did not estimate and validate competing functions.
- Cost deltas were observed, yet I did not infer a reliable cost law or the exact way cost entered the reaction score.
- The single batch-1 HPLC result was used mainly as an illustration of instrument disagreement. Because it was not part of a same-instrument time series, it could not identify kinetics.
- The close material-partition relation among conversion, yield, and byproduct was recognized in K1, but its residuals were not formally compared with propagated instrument uncertainty.

The least reliable blind predictions are Q12, Q04, Q07, and Q08. Q12 extrapolates from a maximum studied target of 410 K and 3600 s to 460 K and 6300 s. Its predicted selectivity of 0.10 and risk near 1 are therefore model-driven guesses, not interpolation. Q04 similarly extrapolates to 450 K. Q07 and Q08 add two-stage order effects that were never studied. My prediction that hot-first treatment in Q08 would preserve more final product than Q07 was explicitly speculative and depends on a sequential-degradation mechanism that the source data did not identify.

Q01/Q02 and Q09/Q10 are also weak because no source batch used a quench. I assigned small quench-associated risk and score differences without direct evidence. A reasonable alternative is that post-heating quench changes neither accumulated risk nor final composition materially, making each pair essentially identical.

All twelve predictions extrapolate to a much smaller volume and much higher catalyst concentration and catalyst-to-reagent ratio. I inferred improved selectivity from batches 2 and 6, but those experiments varied catalyst amount fourfold at fixed scale. They did not establish whether the controlling variable is absolute amount, concentration, molar ratio, or a capped categorical loading function. Consequently, the selectivity and conversion intervals for even the thermally moderate Q03 and Q11 may be too narrow.

Safety intervals may also be too narrow. K1 explicitly said that the inferred relationships might not extrapolate to different concentrations, fill fractions, or scales. The blind predictions nevertheless used a particular assumption: that thermal risk depends mainly on temperature and time, with a smaller material-charge term. If risk instead scales strongly with absolute reactive inventory, I overpredicted risk for the small batches; if it scales with concentration or catalyst-assisted heat release, I may have underpredicted it.

The score intervals are especially vulnerable because K1 admitted that the exact score equation was not identified. Predicting near-zero scores above the safety limit was reasonable for the safe objective, but the public scoring contract did not reveal an explicit multiplicative safety gate. Those score distributions should have been broader or described as mixtures conditional on whether risk crossed 0.35.

Thus the predictions’ broad qualitative ordering may be defensible, but several numerical 80% intervals express more confidence than K1’s declared scope supports. This is most inconsistent for high-temperature, multistage, quenched, and radically rescaled conditions.

## 7. Limitations of the sealed recommendation

Batch 10 was the **sample-in highest-scoring completed experiment**, not a proven optimum. It achieved score 0.1001 and risk 0.2217, outperforming the other eleven observed batches. That fact justifies its selection from the completed set.

It does not establish global optimality because:

- no condition was replicated;
- time was not optimized near 390 K;
- temperature sampling was sparse;
- catalyst loading was not locally optimized in acetonitrile;
- Catalyst A was not compared with B at a matched useful loading;
- concentration and scale were fixed;
- atmosphere, pressure, stirring, and ramp behavior were largely unexplored.

Even local optimality is uncertain. Batch 12 at 400 K scored 0.0946, only about 0.0055 below batch 10. That difference could be sensitive to analytical noise or process variation. K1 therefore correctly called the result a broad 390–400 K productive window rather than a precisely localized optimum.

Repeatability should first be tested with multiple exact repeats of batch 10, reporting the distribution of score, risk, yield, selectivity, byproduct, and degradation rather than only their means. At least three repeats would begin to separate instrument noise from process variability, although more would be preferable.

Local robustness should then be assessed with deliberately small perturbations around the recommendation, such as target temperature changes of ±5–10 K, residence-time changes around 3600 s, modest Catalyst B loading changes, and small stirring perturbations. The key question is not merely whether a neighboring point has a slightly higher mean score, but whether it preserves a comfortable risk margin under variability.

Cross-material robustness requires repeating the local design with other catalyst categories and solvents at matched loadings. The source campaign does not justify transferring the Catalyst B/acetonitrile interaction to Catalyst A–D generally, much less to a named real catalyst.

Cross-world generalization is even more limited. The initial packet defined these catalysts as anonymous latent categorical profiles. A different world or calibration may assign different activity and safety relationships to the same public labels. Generalization would therefore require independent campaigns or a declared invariant mapping; it cannot be inferred from this single world.

The sealed recommendation is consequently best described as a prudent empirical choice among the twelve tested batches. Its main strength is that it combined the highest observed score with appreciable safety margin. Its principal weakness is the absence of replication and local multidimensional validation.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 10 achieved the highest observed public safe-score (0.1001) with safety risk 0.2217, comfortably below the 0.35 limit; hotter batches scored lower and approached the limit.
